- [Handling Fixed and Restricted Molecules](20-handling-fixed-and-restricted-molecules) - Fixed molecule integration

# Polar to Cartesian Coordinate Transformation



This documentation explains the coordinate transformation system that converts molecular position and orientation parameters from a compact polar representation into Cartesian coordinates for the GENCAN optimization algorithm. The transformation enables efficient optimization of molecular packing by reducing the degrees of freedom from 3N Cartesian coordinates per molecule to just 6 parameters (3 translational, 3 rotational) per molecule. This transformation is fundamental to packmol's ability to efficiently solve complex molecular packing problems through gradient-based optimization.

Sources: [polartocart.f90](/src/polartocart.f90#L1-L101), [computef.f90](/src/computef.f90#L37-L73)

## Mathematical Foundations and Representation

The polar representation employs a six-degree-of-freedom parameterization per molecule: three translational parameters representing the center of mass coordinates (xcm, ycm, zcm) and three rotational parameters using Euler angles (β, γ, θ). The canonical molecular geometry is stored in a body-fixed coordinate system relative to each molecule's center of mass, enabling efficient transformations during optimization iterations. This representation reduces the optimization space dimensionality from 3N to 6 per molecule, where N is the number of atoms, while preserving full molecular degrees of freedom.

The transformation from canonical coordinates to global Cartesian coordinates follows the linear equation: **x_cartesian = x_cm + R(β,γ,θ) · x_canonical**, where R is the rotation matrix constructed from Euler angles and x_canonical represents atomic positions in the molecule's reference frame. The canonical coordinates are precomputed from input files and stored in the `coor` array within `compute_data` module, serving as immutable reference geometry throughout the optimization process.

Sources: [polartocart.f90](/src/polartocart.f90#L49-L58), [compute_data.f90](/src/compute_data.f90#L28-L29)

## Core Transformation Algorithms

The transformation system implements three fundamental routines within `polartocart.f90`. The `eulerrmat` subroutine computes the rotation matrix from Euler angles using a specific axis convention where β rotates about the y-axis, γ about the z-axis, and θ about the x-axis. This convention, while non-intuitive from a human perspective, is mathematically consistent throughout the optimization framework. The subroutine computes 9 matrix elements efficiently using trigonometric functions, storing the three orthonormal basis vectors v1, v2, and v3 that constitute the rotation matrix columns.

The `compcart` subroutine performs the actual coordinate transformation by applying the rotation matrix to canonical coordinates and translating to the global center of mass position. This operation is performed atom-by-atom for each molecule during every function and gradient evaluation, making it computationally critical. The transformation formula explicitly computes each Cartesian coordinate as: **x(i) = xcm(i) + Σ[j=1 to 3] xref(j) · vj(i)**, where xref represents canonical coordinates and vj are rotation matrix column vectors.

The third routine, `eulerfixed`, implements an alternative rotation matrix calculation using the human-intuitive convention where β rotates about the x-axis, γ about the y-axis, and θ about the z-axis. This routine is exclusively used for positioning fixed molecules, providing user-friendly rotation specification while maintaining the efficiency of the primary optimization algorithm.

Sources: [polartocart.f90](/src/polartocart.f90#L14-L99), [computef.f90](/src/computef.f90#L54-L72)

## Integration with Optimization Workflow

The coordinate transformation is deeply integrated into packmol's optimization pipeline through the `computef` and `computeg` subroutines. During each objective function evaluation in `computef`, the system iterates through all molecules, extracts the 6 optimization variables (3 center of mass coordinates and 3 Euler angles), computes the rotation matrix via `eulerrmat`, then transforms all atoms of each molecule using `compcart`. The resulting Cartesian coordinates are stored in the `xcart` array for subsequent constraint evaluation and distance calculations.

The transformation process follows a structured indexing scheme where center of mass variables occupy indices 1 through 3·n_totmol, and Euler angle variables occupy indices 3·n_totmol+1 through 6·n_totmol. This indexing enables efficient variable extraction during transformation. The transformed coordinates are immediately used for cell indexing assignment, constraint violation evaluation, and intermolecular distance calculations within the same function call, minimizing memory access overhead.

During gradient computation in `computeg`, the transformation is repeated identically to ensure coordinate consistency with the function evaluation, enabling accurate gradient calculation through the chain rule. The Cartesian gradients computed from distance and constraint violations must be propagated back to the polar parameter space, requiring the rotation matrix and its partial derivatives.

Sources: [computef.f90](/src/computef.f90#L37-L109), [computeg.f90](/src/computeg.f90#L39-L96)

## Dual Rotation Matrix Architecture

Packmol employs a sophisticated dual rotation matrix architecture to balance human usability with computational efficiency. The primary rotation matrix, computed by `eulerrmat`, uses an unconventional axis sequence optimized for derivative calculations and efficient gradient propagation. The secondary rotation matrix, computed by `eulerfixed`, uses standard Euler angle conventions for user-specified fixed molecules.

> [!TIP]
> The dual matrix architecture eliminates the need for derivative recomputation when adopting human-friendly rotation conventions. Fixed molecules use `eulerfixed` for position specification, while the optimization variables continue using `eulerrmat`, maintaining gradient efficiency without requiring analytical derivative re-derivation.

This architectural separation is evident in the `initial` subroutine where fixed molecules bypass the polar-to-Cartesian transformation pipeline entirely. Fixed atoms are copied directly from canonical coordinates to Cartesian coordinates without rotation, marked with the `fixedatom` flag, and excluded from optimization. This design choice enables users to specify fixed molecule orientations using intuitive rotation parameters while preserving the mathematical consistency of the optimization framework.

The rotation matrix orthonormality properties (columns v1, v2, v3 form a right-handed orthonormal basis) are mathematically enforced through the trigonometric construction in both routines, ensuring coordinate transformations preserve interatomic distances and molecular geometry integrity.

Sources: [polartocart.f90](/src/polartocart.f90#L6-L69), [initial.f90](/src/initial.f90#L140-L150)

## Gradient Computation and Chain Rule

The most mathematically sophisticated aspect of the transformation system is gradient propagation from Cartesian coordinate space to polar parameter space using the chain rule. In `computeg`, after computing Cartesian gradients for all atoms, the system must transform these gradients back to gradient components for the 6 molecular parameters: ∂f/∂xcm, ∂f/∂ycm, ∂f/∂zcm, ∂f/∂β, ∂f/∂γ, and ∂f/∂θ.

The translational gradients are straightforward: **∂f/∂xcm_i = Σ[∂f/∂x_cartesian_j]** summed over all atoms j in molecule i, reflecting the fact that moving the center of mass translates all atoms equally. The rotational gradients require more complex calculations involving partial derivatives of the rotation matrix elements with respect to each Euler angle. The gradient components for each rotation angle are computed as: **∂f/∂θ = Σ[j,k] ∂f/∂x_cartesian[j,k] · (coor[j,1]·∂v1[k]/∂θ + coor[j,2]·∂v2[k]/∂θ + coor[j,3]·∂v3[k]/∂θ)**.

The partial derivatives of rotation matrix columns (∂v1/∂β, ∂v1/∂γ, ∂v1/∂θ, etc.) are computed analytically from the trigonometric expressions used in `eulerrmat`. These 27 partial derivative values (3 matrix columns × 3 angles × 3 spatial components) are precomputed for each molecule before the gradient summation loop, minimizing redundant trigonometric calculations. This analytical gradient computation ensures second-order convergence of the GENCAN optimization algorithm.

Sources: [computeg.f90](/src/computef.f90#L145-L241), [polartocart.f90](/src/polartocart.f90#L14-L41)

## Performance and Computational Considerations

The coordinate transformation system is a critical performance bottleneck due to its execution frequency during optimization. Each function evaluation requires transforming all atoms of all molecules, and each gradient evaluation repeats this transformation. For systems with thousands of molecules and atoms, this represents millions of coordinate transformations per optimization iteration.

The implementation addresses performance through several strategies. First, trigonometric computations (sines and cosines) are performed once per molecule and reused for all atoms, avoiding redundant calculations. Second, the transformation uses explicit vector operations rather than matrix multiplication for the coordinate transformation, reducing intermediate array allocations. Third, the rotation matrix columns are computed in place without temporary arrays, minimizing memory bandwidth requirements.

The cell indexing integration within the transformation loop in `computef` amortizes the cost of cell assignment across the transformation operation. As atoms are transformed, their cell indices are computed immediately, and they are added to the appropriate linked lists in a single pass through the atom array. This tight coupling between transformation and spatial indexing reduces loop overhead and cache misses.

Sources: [computef.f90](/src/computef.f90#L63-L101), [polartocart.f90](/src/polartocart.f90#L49-L58)

## Rotation Convention Comparison

The choice between the two rotation matrix implementations represents a fundamental trade-off between computational efficiency and human interpretability:

| Aspect | eulerrmat (Optimization) | eulerfixed (Fixed Molecules) |
|--------|-------------------------|------------------------------|
| β Rotation Axis | Y-axis | X-axis |
| γ Rotation Axis | Z-axis | Y-axis |
| θ Rotation Axis | X-axis | Z-axis |
| Primary Use | Optimization variables | User-specified fixed molecules |
| Derivative Efficiency | Optimized for chain rule | Not used in gradients |
| Human Interpretability | Low (non-intuitive) | High (standard convention) |
| Integration | computef, computeg, initial | initial (fixed molecules only) |

> [!TIP]
> The unconventional rotation convention in `eulerrmat` is deliberate and mathematically motivated. It simplifies the partial derivative expressions required for gradient propagation, reducing computational cost in the optimization inner loop where gradients are computed thousands of times.

This dual approach enables users to specify fixed molecule positions and orientations using intuitive rotation parameters while the optimization algorithm operates efficiently with mathematically convenient parameterizations internally.

Sources: [polartocart.f90](/src/polartocart.f90#L6-L99)

## Transformation Flow Architecture

The following diagram illustrates the complete data flow from polar parameters through transformation to Cartesian coordinates and back to polar gradients:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Optimization Variables<br/>x_cm: 3·n_totmol<br/>Euler angles: 3·n_totmol] --> B[Extract Parameters<br/>per molecule]
    B --> C[Compute Rotation Matrix<br/>eulerrmat: Rβ,γ,θ]
    C --> D[Transform Atoms<br/>compcart: x_cart = x_cm + R·x_ref]
    D --> E[Cell Indexing<br/>setcell]
    D --> F[Constraint Evaluation<br/>comprest]
    D --> G[Distance Calculation<br/>fparc]
    
    E & F & G --> H[Cartesian Gradients<br/>gxcar]
    H --> I[Chain Rule Propagation<br/>∂f/∂θ = Σ gxcar · ∂R/∂θ · x_ref]
    I --> J[Polar Gradients<br/>∂f/∂x_cm, ∂f/∂β, ∂f/∂γ, ∂f/∂θ]
    
    K[Fixed Molecules] --> L[eulerfixed Matrix<br/>User-friendly convention]
    L --> M[Direct Copy<br/>xcart = coor]
    
    J --> N[GENCAN Optimizer<br/>Next iteration]
```

Sources: [computef.f90](/src/computef.f90#L37-L109), [computeg.f90](/src/computeg.f90#L145-L241), [initial.f90](/src/initial.f90#L140-L150)

## Next Steps

Understanding the polar to Cartesian coordinate transformation provides the foundation for exploring packmol's optimization architecture. The next logical step is to examine [Distance Constraints and Overlap Detection](17-distance-constraints-and-overlap-detection) to understand how transformed coordinates are used for molecular packing evaluation. For deeper insight into the mathematical foundations, refer to [Molecular Coordinate Systems: Baricenter and Euler Angles](13-molecular-coordinate-systems-baricenter-and-euler-angles). The optimization algorithm that drives these transformations is detailed in [GENCAN Optimization Method Overview](9-gencan-optimization-method-overview).

# Center of Mass Calculations



The Center of Mass (COM) calculation system in Packmol serves as the foundational coordinate normalization mechanism for molecular packing operations. This system establishes a consistent reference frame where each molecule's center of mass is positioned at the origin prior to optimization, ensuring predictable and efficient packing behavior. The COM subsystem integrates with spatial constraints, rotational dynamics, and the optimization algorithm to enable precise molecular positioning in complex systems.

## Architectural Overview

The COM calculation architecture operates as a preprocessing pipeline that transforms raw molecular coordinates into a standardized coordinate system. The system is anchored by the `cenmass()` subroutine in [cenmass.f90](src/cenmass.f90#L11-L103), which executes immediately after input parsing and before optimization initialization. This critical placement ensures that all subsequent operations—initial configuration generation, constraint evaluation, and optimization—operate on COM-centered coordinates.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input["Input Phase"]
        A[Read Input File] --> B[Parse Keywords]
        B --> C[Load Coordinates]
        C --> D[Load Atomic Masses]
    end
    
    subgraph COMProcessing["COM Processing"]
        D --> E[Call cenmass]
        E --> F{COM Required?}
        F -->|fixed keyword| G[Skip COM Translation]
        F -->|centerofmass keyword| H[Compute COM]
        H --> I[Translate to Origin]
    end
    
    subgraph Optimization["Optimization Phase"]
        I --> J[Build Initial Config]
        J --> K[Apply Spatial Constraints]
        K --> L[GENCAN Optimization]
    end
    
    subgraph Output["Output Phase"]
        L --> M[Apply Final Transformations]
        M --> N[Write Output Coordinates]
    end
```

The architecture reveals three key integration points: the input parsing stage in [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L104-L108) where COM calculations are triggered, the optimization loop in [computef.f90](src/computef.f90#L52-L72) where COM-centered coordinates are reconstructed during function evaluation, and the coordinate transformation system that enables efficient molecular rotation and translation operations.

## COM Computation Algorithm

The core COM computation implements a weighted average calculation across all atoms within each molecule type. The algorithm processes molecules independently, computing three key values: the total mass (`totm`), the mass-weighted coordinate sum (`cm`), and the final normalized COM position. The mathematical foundation is expressed as:

**COM Calculation Formula:**
```
COM_i = (Σ_j m_j × r_j) / (Σ_j m_j)
```

where `COM_i` is the center of mass vector for molecule type `i`, `m_j` is the atomic mass of atom `j`, and `r_j` is the position vector of atom `j`.

The implementation in [cenmass.f90](src/cenmass.f90#L64-L84) follows a three-phase approach. First, the total mass for each molecule type is accumulated by iterating over all atoms and summing their atomic masses from the `amass` array. Second, the mass-weighted position vectors are computed by multiplying each atom's coordinates by its mass and accumulating the sum. Finally, the COM is normalized by dividing the weighted sums by the total mass.

**Critical Implementation Detail:** The atomic coordinate array `coor` stores relative positions from the molecule's COM reference point, not absolute positions. After COM calculation, the subroutine immediately translates all atom coordinates by subtracting the COM vector, effectively moving the COM to the origin [cenmass.f90](src/cenmass.f90#L86-L98). This transformation is fundamental to the molecular coordinate system described in [Molecular Coordinate Systems: Baricenter and Euler Angles](13-molecular-coordinate-systems-baricenter-and-euler-angles).

> [!TIP]
> The COM translation is performed in-place on the global `coor` array. This means subsequent references to `coor` implicitly assume COM-centered coordinates, and any external coordinate files must be interpreted in this context when analyzing optimization results.

## COM Control Through Input Keywords

Packmol provides two complementary keywords for controlling COM behavior at the molecule level: `fixed` and `centerofmass` (or `center`). These keywords are specified within structure blocks and enable fine-grained control over which molecules undergo COM translation.

### Keyword Behavior Matrix

| Keyword | Default State | COM Translation | Typical Use Case |
|---------|---------------|-----------------|------------------|
| `fixed` | Disabled | Disabled (skip) | Anchor molecules at specified positions |
| `centerofmass` | Enabled | Enabled | Standard free molecules requiring COM centering |
| Neither specified | Enabled | Enabled | Default behavior for free molecules |

The keyword processing logic in [cenmass.f90](src/cenmass.f90#L33-L54) implements a priority system. Initially, all molecule types are marked for COM translation (`domass(itype) = .true.`). The `fixed` keyword then selectively disables COM translation for molecules anchored at specific positions. The `centerofmass` keyword can override this behavior, explicitly enabling COM translation even for molecules that might otherwise be fixed.

### Input Syntax Examples

**Standard COM Translation (Default Behavior):**
```
structure water.pdb
  number 100
  inside box 0. 0. 0. 40. 40. 40.
end structure
```

**Explicit COM Translation:**
```
structure benzene.pdb
  number 2
  inside box 0. 0. 0. 40. 40. 40.
  centerofmass
end structure
```

**Fixed Molecule with COM Disabled:**
```
structure protein.pdb
  number 1
  fixed 20. 20. 20. 0. 0. 0.
end structure
```

**Fixed Molecule with COM Explicitly Enabled:**
```
structure ion.pdb
  number 1
  fixed 0. 0. -1. 0. 0. 0.
  centerofmass
end structure
```

The example from [toy_with_fixed.inp](testing/input_files/toy_with_fixed.inp#L8-L9) demonstrates a use case where fixed ions are explicitly centered using the `centerofmass` keyword, while the `fixed` keyword positions them at specific coordinates. This combination is useful for creating ionic pairs or defining reference points in simulation systems.

## COM Integration with Optimization Variables

The optimization vector `x` contains both translational and rotational degrees of freedom for each molecule. The COM system directly contributes to the translational components, which represent the position of each molecule's center of mass in the simulation space. This separation of concerns enables efficient optimization: the algorithm manipulates COM positions directly without needing to account for internal molecular geometry.

### Optimization Variable Structure

The optimization vector `x` is organized as follows:
- **Components 1 to `ntotmol × 3`**: COM coordinates (x, y, z) for each molecule
- **Components `ntotmol × 3 + 1` to end**: Euler angles (β, γ, θ) for rotational degrees of freedom

During each function evaluation in [computef.f90](src/computef.f90#L52-L72), the COM is extracted from the optimization vector:
```fortran
xcm = x(ilubar+1:ilubar+3)
```

This COM vector (`xcm`) is then combined with the rotation matrix (derived from Euler angles) and the COM-centered relative coordinates (`coor`) to reconstruct the absolute atomic positions:
```fortran
call compcart(xcart(icart,1:3), xcm, coor(idatom,1:3), v1, v2, v3)
```

The transformation from optimization variables to Cartesian coordinates is defined as:
```
r_absolute = r_COM + R × r_relative
```

where `r_absolute` is the final atomic position, `r_COM` is the center of mass position from the optimization vector, `R` is the rotation matrix from Euler angles, and `r_relative` is the COM-centered coordinate from the `coor` array.

## COM System Data Flow

The COM calculation system processes data through multiple arrays and data structures maintained across the program. Understanding this data flow is critical for debugging and extending the COM functionality.

### Key Data Structures

| Array | Module | Dimensions | Purpose in COM System |
|-------|--------|------------|----------------------|
| `coor` | compute_data | (ntotat, 3) | COM-centered relative coordinates |
| `amass` | input | (ntotat) | Atomic masses for COM weighting |
| `idfirst` | compute_data | (ntype) | Index of first atom for each type |
| `natoms` | compute_data | (ntype) | Number of atoms per molecule type |
| `xcm` | local | (3) | Current COM position during optimization |
| `xcart` | compute_data | (ntotat, 3) | Reconstructed absolute coordinates |

> [!TIP]
> The `coor` array is permanently modified by COM translation. If you need to access original coordinates, you must reload them from input files before calling `cenmass()`.

### COM Data Transformation Pipeline

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Stage1["Stage 1: Input Loading"]
        A[PDB/XYZ File] --> B[coor array<br/>Original Coordinates]
        C[Atom Masses] --> D[amass array]
    end
    
    subgraph Stage2["Stage 2: COM Calculation"]
        B --> E[Compute Weighted Sum]
        D --> E
        E --> F[Normalize by Total Mass]
        F --> G[COM Vector]
    end
    
    subgraph Stage3["Stage 3: Translation"]
        B --> H[Subtract COM]
        G --> H
        H --> I[coor array<br/>COM-Centered]
    end
    
    subgraph Stage4["Stage 4: Optimization"]
        I --> J[Function Evaluation]
        J --> K[Optimization Vector x<br/>Contains COM Positions]
        K --> L[Reconstruction with compcart]
    end
```

This pipeline ensures that the COM system operates consistently throughout the packing process. The transition from Stage 3 to Stage 4 is particularly important: once coordinates are COM-centered, they remain in that frame throughout optimization, with absolute positions reconstructed on-the-fly during function evaluations.

## COM in Periodic Boundary Conditions

When periodic boundary conditions (PBC) are enabled, the COM system must account for the periodic nature of the simulation box. The COM calculation itself remains unchanged—it operates on the COM-centered relative coordinates stored in `coor`. However, the optimization variables (COM positions stored in `x`) and the reconstructed absolute coordinates must respect PBC boundaries.

The COM system interacts with PBC through several mechanisms described in [Periodic Boundary Conditions (PBC) Configuration](8-periodic-boundary-conditions-pbc-configuration):

1. **Initial Configuration**: The initial COM positions generated in [initial.f90](src/initial.f90#L93-L95) respect the PBC boundaries defined by `pbc_min` and `pbc_max`.
2. **Distance Calculations**: Pairwise distance computations in [fparc.f90](src/fparc.f90) apply minimum image conventions, ensuring that COM-based constraints are evaluated correctly across periodic boundaries.
3. **Fixed Molecules**: Fixed molecules must have all atoms within the PBC box after COM translation and rotation [initial.f90](src/initial.f90#L152-L162).

A critical validation occurs when fixed molecules are placed: the system verifies that all atoms of fixed molecules remain within the PBC boundaries after applying the COM transformation and any specified rotation. If any atom falls outside the defined PBC region, the program terminates with an error, preventing invalid initial configurations.

## Performance Considerations

The COM calculation is performed exactly once per molecule type during initialization, making it computationally negligible compared to the optimization loop. The algorithm complexity is O(N) where N is the total number of atoms, as each atom is visited exactly once during the mass summation and coordinate transformation phases.

However, the COM system has important implications for overall optimization performance:

1. **Reduced Search Space**: By centering molecules at their COM, the optimization algorithm operates on translational and rotational degrees of freedom separately, reducing the dimensionality of the search problem from 3N (N atoms) to 6 (3 translational + 3 rotational per molecule).

2. **Efficient Rotation Operations**: COM-centered coordinates enable efficient rotation matrix application without needing to recompute the COM during each rotation operation.

3. **Constraint Evaluation**: Spatial constraints defined in terms of COM positions (such as box or sphere constraints) are evaluated directly against optimization variables, avoiding repeated coordinate transformations.

The performance benefits are most pronounced in large systems with many molecules, where the reduced search space and efficient coordinate transformations significantly accelerate convergence.

## COM Calculation Limitations and Edge Cases

The COM system assumes accurate atomic mass data and well-defined molecular geometries. Several edge cases require special consideration:

### Zero-Mass or Undefined Masses

If atomic masses are not provided in input files or are set to zero, the COM calculation becomes mathematically undefined. The implementation protects against this by accumulating total mass first [cenmass.f90](src/cenmass.f90#L64-L71). If `totm(itype)` is zero, the subsequent division would cause division-by-zero errors. In practice, Packmol requires valid mass data for all atoms, and input parsing should validate mass values before COM calculation.

### Single-Atom Molecules

For single-atom molecules, the COM calculation is trivial: the COM is simply the atom's position. The algorithm handles this correctly, as the weighted sum contains a single term and the total mass is that atom's mass. After COM translation, the single atom's relative coordinate becomes (0, 0, 0), and its absolute position is determined entirely by the optimization variable.

### Degenerate Geometries

Molecules with degenerate geometries (all atoms at the same position) pose no algorithmic problems for COM calculation but represent physically unrealistic configurations. The COM calculation correctly computes the geometric center, and the subsequent translation positions the molecule at the origin. However, such configurations typically cause problems in subsequent overlap detection and constraint satisfaction.

## Integration with Constraint Enforcement

The COM system forms the foundation for spatial constraint enforcement. All spatial constraints—boxes, spheres, cylinders, planes—operate on COM positions for molecular placement. The constraint evaluation subsystem described in [Distance Constraints and Overlap Detection](17-distance-constraints-and-overlap-detection) uses COM positions from optimization variables to verify constraint satisfaction.

For example, when placing a molecule inside a box, the constraint is evaluated as:
```
x_min ≤ COM_x ≤ x_max
y_min ≤ COM_y ≤ y_max
z_min ≤ COM_z ≤ z_max
```

Because the optimization vector contains COM positions directly, these constraints are evaluated without needing to reconstruct atomic coordinates. This efficiency is a key advantage of the COM-centered coordinate system.

For constraints that operate on individual atoms (such as `displacement 2.0` constraints), the system first reconstructs absolute atomic positions using the COM and rotation matrix, then evaluates the constraint on individual atoms. This dual approach—COM-based for molecular constraints, atom-based for atomic constraints—provides maximum flexibility while maintaining computational efficiency.

## Next Steps

Understanding the COM system provides the foundation for exploring several interconnected concepts:

- [Molecular Coordinate Systems: Baricenter and Euler Angles](13-molecular-coordinate-systems-baricenter-and-euler-angles) describes how COM positions combine with rotational parameters to reconstruct absolute molecular positions
- [Distance Constraints and Overlap Detection](17-distance-constraints-and-overlap-detection) explains how COM positions are used in spatial constraint evaluation
- [Handling Fixed and Restricted Molecules](20-handling-fixed-and-restricted-molecules) details the interaction between COM calculations and fixed molecule placement
- [Objective Function Design in computef.f90](10-objective-function-design-in-computef-f90) shows how COM variables contribute to the optimization objective function

The COM system is fundamental to Packmol's efficiency and correctness. Mastering its behavior is essential for understanding the entire packing optimization pipeline and for debugging complex packing configurations.

# Handling Fixed and Restricted Molecules



PackMOL provides sophisticated mechanisms for controlling molecular placement through fixed positioning and spatial restrictions. These capabilities enable precise molecular assembly for complex systems ranging from simple mixtures to elaborate biomolecular assemblies.

## Fixed Molecules: Absolute Positioning

Fixed molecules provide exact control over molecular placement by specifying both position and orientation. The `fixed` constraint takes six parameters: three translational coordinates (x, y, z) and three Euler angles (α, β, γ) defining molecular rotation.

**Syntax**: `fixed x y z alpha beta gamma`

For example, to place a water molecule at the origin with a specific orientation:

```
structure ./structure_files/water.pdb
  number 1
  fixed 0. 0. 0. 45. 45. 45.
end structure
```

Sources: [getinp.f90](testing/input_files/only_one_fixed.inp#L1-L11), [getinp.f90](src/getinp.f90#L540-L548)

The implementation distinguishes fixed molecules from restricted ones through a dedicated data structure. When the `fix` flag is enabled, fixed atoms are loaded directly from structure files into the `xcart` array and marked with `fixedatom(icart) = .true.` in [initial.f90](src/initial.f90#L132-L139). These atoms participate in distance calculations to prevent overlaps with movable molecules, but their positions remain immutable throughout optimization.

**PBC Compatibility**: When periodic boundary conditions are enabled, PackMOL validates that all fixed atoms reside within the simulation box boundaries [initial.f90](src/initial.f90#L140-L150). This prevents simulation artifacts from molecules spanning multiple periodic images.

## Spatial Restrictions: Constrained Placement

Spatial restrictions define regions where molecules must reside. PackMOL supports multiple geometric constraint types, each with a unique identifier in the `ityperest` array:

**Constraint Types**:

| Type | Keyword | Parameters | Description |
|------|---------|------------|-------------|
| 2 | `inside cube` | xc, yc, zc, length | Center coordinates + cube side length |
| 3 | `inside box` | xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax | Opposing corner coordinates |
| 4 | `inside sphere` | xc, yc, zc, radius | Center + radius |
| 5 | `inside ellipsoid` | xc, yc, zc, a, b, c, semiaxis | Center + three semiaxes + scale factor |
| 6 | `outside cube` | xc, yc, zc, length | Excludes volume within cube |
| 7 | `outside box` | xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax | Excludes volume within box |
| 8 | `outside sphere` | xc, yc, zc, radius | Excludes volume within sphere |
| 9 | `outside ellipsoid` | xc, yc, zc, a, b, c, semiaxis | Excludes volume within ellipsoid |
| 10 | `above plane` | nx, ny, nz, d | Normal vector components + distance |
| 11 | `below plane` | nx, ny, nz, d | Normal vector components + distance |
| 12 | `inside cylinder` | xc, yc, zc, nx, ny, nz, radius, height | Axis point + direction vector + dimensions |
| 13 | `outside cylinder` | xc, yc, zc, nx, ny, nz, radius, height | Excludes volume within cylinder |
| 14 | `above xygauss` | xc, yc, zc, σx, σy, A | Gaussian surface constraint |
| 15 | `below xygauss` | xc, yc, zc, σx, σy, A | Gaussian surface constraint |

Sources: [getinp.f90](src/getinp.f90#L552-L730)

## Constraint Enforcement Architecture

The constraint enforcement system operates through three core components working in sequence:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Input Parsing] --> B[Constraint Registration]
    B --> C[Initial Placement via restmol]
    C --> D[Objective Function Evaluation]
    D --> E[Gradient Computation]
    E --> F[GENCAN Optimization]
    
    subgraph B [Constraint Registration]
        B1[Read fixed parameters]
        B2[Read spatial constraints]
        B3[Store in restpars array]
        B4[Assign ityperest identifiers]
    end
    
    subgraph C [Initial Placement]
        C1[Restmol: isolate molecule]
        C2[pgencan optimization]
        C3[Apply constraint-only objective]
        C4[Restore full system]
    end
    
    subgraph D [Objective Function]
        D1[Transform coordinates]
        D2[Call comprest for each atom]
        D3[Accumulate penalty terms]
        D4[Track maximum violation]
    end
    
    subgraph E [Gradient Computation]
        E1[Compute constraint gradients]
        E2[Call gwalls for each constraint]
        E3[Apply chain rule]
        E4[Return to GENCAN]
    end
```

## The Restmol Subroutine: Isolated Constraint Satisfaction

The `restmol` subroutine in [restmol.f90](src/restmol.f90#L19-L71) implements a powerful technique for satisfying spatial constraints: it temporarily reduces the optimization problem to a single molecule.

The process works as follows:

1. **State Preservation**: Save the global problem state including molecule counts and coordinate arrays
2. **Problem Reduction**: Set `ntotmol = 1` and `nmols(itype) = 1` to focus on the target molecule
3. **Type Isolation**: Enable only the current molecule type via `comptype(i) = .true.` for the target and `.false.` for others
4. **Constraint Solution**: Either evaluate the constraint penalty or invoke `pgencan` to solve the placement problem
5. **State Restoration**: Return original molecule counts and coordinate arrays

This isolation strategy is crucial for systems with complex constraints. By solving each molecule's placement independently before considering intermolecular distances, PackMOL avoids local minima where molecules might become trapped in overlapping configurations while trying to satisfy multiple spatial constraints simultaneously.

Sources: [restmol.f90](src/restmol.f90#L19-L71)

## Constraint Penalty Functions

Each spatial constraint type implements a penalty function in `comprest.f90` that returns zero when atoms satisfy the constraint and positive values proportional to violation severity.

**Inside Constraints** (Types 2, 3): Use squared distance penalties from boundaries. For a box constraint with bounds [xmin, xmax], the penalty is:

```fortran
a1 = dmin1(xcart(icart,1) - xmin, 0.d0)
f = f + scale*(a1 * a1)
```

This penalizes atoms with x < xmin. A symmetric calculation penalizes x > xmax. The `scale` parameter (typically 10²) determines penalty severity.

Sources: [comprest.f90](src/comprest.f90#L26-L37)

**Spherical Constraints** (Types 4, 8): Compute radial distance from sphere center. For an inside sphere constraint:

```fortran
w = (xcart(icart,1)-restpars(irest,1))² + 
    (xcart(icart,2)-restpars(irest,2))² + 
    (xcart(icart,3)-restpars(irest,3))² - 
    restpars(irest,4)²
a1 = dmax1(w,0.d0)
f = f + scale2*a1*a1
```

The penalty activates when the radial distance exceeds the sphere radius.

Sources: [comprest.f90](src/comprest.f90#L38-L44)

**Planar Constraints** (Types 10, 11): Use dot product of position with normal vector. For `above plane`:

```fortran
w = restpars(irest,1)*xcart(icart,1) + 
    restpars(irest,2)*xcart(icart,2) + 
    restpars(irest,3)*xcart(icart,3) - 
    restpars(irest,4)
a1 = dmin1(w,0.d0)
f = f + scale * a1*a1
```

This computes signed distance from the plane and penalizes violations.

Sources: [comprest.f90](src/comprest.f90#L115-L121)

**Cylindrical Constraints** (Types 12, 13): Decompose position into components parallel and perpendicular to the cylinder axis. The penalty considers both radial confinement and axial bounds:

```fortran
! Radial component
d = (a1 - v1*w)² + (a2 - v2*w)² + (a3 - v3*w)²
! Combined penalty for inside cylinder
f = f + scale2 * (dmax1(-w, 0.d0)² + 
                  dmax1(w - height, 0.d0)² + 
                  dmax1(d - radius², 0.d0)²)
```

This enforces three conditions simultaneously: axial lower bound, axial upper bound, and radial confinement.

Sources: [comprest.f90](src/comprest.f90#L133-L144)

## Initial Placement Strategy

The initialization phase in [initial.f90](src/initial.f90#L164-L202) employs a two-stage approach for handling constrained molecules:

1. **Constraint-Only Optimization**: With `init1 = .true.`, PackMOL evaluates only spatial constraints (ignoring intermolecular distances) and optimizes each molecule type sequentially using `swaptype` to isolate types and `pgencan` for optimization

2. **Convergence Validation**: If `frest > precision` after `nloop0_type(itype)` iterations, the system reports failure, indicating that the constraints themselves are unsatisfiable

> [!TIP]
> The constraint-only optimization phase is critical for detecting impossible configurations early. If molecules cannot satisfy their spatial constraints even without considering intermolecular distances, the problem specification itself contains a geometric inconsistency that must be corrected before distance tolerances can be addressed.

Sources: [initial.f90](src/initial.f90#L164-L202)

## Fixed vs Restricted Molecules: Key Differences

Understanding the distinction between these two concepts is essential for effective use:

| Aspect | Fixed Molecules | Restricted Molecules |
|--------|----------------|---------------------|
| **Syntax** | `fixed x y z α β γ` | `inside/outside [geometry] parameters` |
| **Degrees of Freedom** | Zero (fully specified) | 6 (translation + rotation) |
| **Optimization** | None (coordinates constant) | Full GENCAN optimization |
| **Storage** | Special `fix` flag and `fixedatom` array | Standard optimization variables |
| **PBC Requirements** | Must be within simulation box | Automatically constrained to PBC region |
| **Use Case** | Reference structures, anchor molecules | Solvent shells, partitioned regions |

## Gradient Computation for Constraints

Analytical gradients for spatial constraints are computed in `computeg.f90` through the `gwalls` subroutine. This enables efficient optimization by providing exact sensitivity information to the GENCAN solver.

For each atom, the system loops through all applicable constraints [computeg.f90](src/computeg.f90#L56-L60):

```fortran
do iratcount = 1, nratom(icart)
   irest = iratom(icart,iratcount)
   call gwalls(icart,irest)
end do
```

The `gwalls` subroutine computes derivatives of the penalty function with respect to Cartesian coordinates, which are then transformed via chain rule to obtain derivatives with respect to the baricenter position and Euler angles (the actual optimization variables).

Sources: [computeg.f90](src/computeg.f90#L56-L60)

## Practical Example: Toy System with Fixed Molecules

The test file `toy_with_fixed.inp` demonstrates combining fixed and restricted molecules:

```
structure ./structure_files/SOD.pdb
  number 1 
  fixed 0. 0. -1. 0. 0. 0.
  centerofmass
end structure

structure ./structure_files/SOD.pdb
  number 1 
  fixed 0. 0. 1. 0. 0. 0.
  centerofmass
end structure

structure ./structure_files/CLA.pdb
  number 1
  inside box -1.0 -1.0 -2.0 1.0 1.0 3.0
end structure
```

This configuration places two sodium ions at fixed positions (z = -1 and z = +1) while allowing a chloride ion to occupy any position within the specified box region. The system demonstrates how fixed molecules can create asymmetric environments around which flexible molecules organize.

Sources: [toy_with_fixed.inp](testing/input_files/toy_with_fixed.inp#L1-L27)

## Performance Considerations

Fixed molecules provide computational advantages by reducing the optimization problem dimension. With `nfix` fixed molecules, the optimization variables decrease from `6 × (nfix + nmove)` to `6 × nmove`, significantly accelerating convergence for large systems.

Restricted molecules add computational overhead through penalty evaluations and gradient calculations for each constraint. However, the constraint system is designed to be efficient:
- Constraints are pre-assigned to atoms during input parsing via the `iratom` array
- Only applicable constraints are evaluated for each atom
- Analytical gradients avoid numerical differentiation overhead

> [!TIP]
> When designing systems with many constraints, prefer geometric primitives (box, sphere, cylinder) over complex composite regions. Simple constraints enable more efficient evaluation and typically lead to better convergence properties.

## Integration with Distance Constraints

Spatial constraints work in conjunction with distance tolerance constraints. The objective function combines both components [computef.f90](src/computef.f90#L24-L36):

```fortran
call comprest(icart,fplus)
f = f + fplus
frest = dmax1(frest,fplus)
```

The total objective includes:
- **Spatial constraint penalties** (via `comprest`)
- **Distance violation penalties** (via `fparc` function for neighbor pairs)
- **Scale factors** (`scale` ~ 10² for spatial, implicit for distance)

The optimization algorithm simultaneously satisfies both categories of constraints, with spatial constraints typically dominating during early iterations when molecules are far apart.

Sources: [computef.f90](src/computef.f90#L24-L36)

## Next Steps

For deeper understanding of related topics:

- [Spatial Constraints Syntax (Box, Sphere, Plane, Cylinder)](5-spatial-constraints-syntax-box-sphere-plane-cylinder) - Detailed syntax examples and geometric definitions
- [Molecular Coordinate Systems: Baricenter and Euler Angles](13-molecular-coordinate-systems-baricenter-and-euler-angles) - Mathematical foundation for position/rotation variables
- [GENCAN Optimization Method Overview](9-gencan-optimization-method-overview) - The optimization algorithm that solves constraint problems
- [Objective Function Design in computef.f90](10-objective-function-design-in-computef-f90) - How penalties combine into the total objective

# Main Program Execution Flow in packmol.f90



This documentation provides a comprehensive analysis of Packmol's main program execution architecture. The `packmol.f90` file serves as the orchestrator that coordinates input parsing, initialization, optimization, and output generation for molecular packing simulations. Understanding this flow is essential for developers seeking to extend functionality or debug complex packing scenarios.

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L34-L980)

## Program Architecture Overview

Packmol employs a modular architecture where the main program coordinates multiple specialized subsystems. The execution flow follows a carefully designed sequence that separates initialization, configuration, and optimization into distinct phases. This modular design enables clear separation of concerns while maintaining efficient data flow between components.

The program is structured around the optimization problem of placing molecules within spatial constraints while avoiding overlaps. Each molecule is parameterized by 6 degrees of freedom (3 translation + 3 rotation), forming the optimization variables that GENCAN manipulates to minimize the objective function.

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L34-L46), [usegencan.f90](src/usegencan.f90#L8-L18)

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[Start] --> B[Title Display]
    B --> C[Command-line Parsing]
    C --> D[Set Dimensions]
    D --> E[Memory Allocation]
    E --> F[Read Input File]
    F --> G[Center of Mass Calculation]
    G --> H[Fixed Molecule Processing]
    H --> I[Parameter Setup Phase]
    I --> J{Any Free Molecules?}
    J -->|No| K[Output Fixed Molecules]
    K --> L[Stop]
    J -->|Yes| M[Initial Configuration]
    M --> N{Check Mode?}
    N -->|Yes| O[Output Initial Point]
    O --> L
    N -->|No| P[Main Packing Loop]
    P --> Q[Output Results]
    Q --> L
```

## Phase 1: Program Initialization

The initialization phase establishes the foundation for all subsequent operations by setting up memory structures, reading user input, and performing initial coordinate transformations.

**Module Dependencies**: The program begins by importing essential modules that define global data structures and utility functions. Key modules include `exit_codes` for standardized error handling, `sizes` for array dimensioning, `compute_data` for coordinate storage, `cli_parser` for command-line interface, `input` for parameter management, `usegencan` for optimization interfaces, and specialized modules for sorting and aesthetics.

**Startup Sequence**: The first executable action displays program header information via `call title()` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L83), followed by `call parse_command_line_args()` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L87) which processes command-line arguments such as input file specification and debugging flags. The `call setsizes()` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L91) routine dynamically determines array sizes based on input file contents.

**Memory Allocation**: Critical arrays are allocated after dimensioning, including the `fixed(ntype)` array tracking immobile molecules, the optimization variable array `x(nn)` containing 6 degrees of freedom per molecule, and working arrays `xprint(nn)` and `xfull(nn)` for state management [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L95).

**Input Parsing**: The `call getinp()` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L104) subroutine reads the input file, parsing molecule definitions, spatial constraints, and optimization parameters. This routine populates the `input` module's data structures with all user-specified configuration.

**Coordinate Centering**: The `call cenmass()` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L108) routine centers each molecule at its center of mass, establishing a consistent reference frame for rotational operations and constraint applications.

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L36-L112), [input.f90](src/input.f90#L9-L82)

## Phase 2: Fixed Molecule Processing

Fixed molecules are molecules that remain stationary throughout the optimization process, serving as reference structures around which other molecules are arranged.

**Identification and Positioning**: The program iterates through restrictions (`nrest`) to identify fixed molecule specifications indicated by `ityperest(irest).eq.1` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L118). For each fixed molecule, the program retrieves the target position (`xcm`) from `restpars(irest,1:3)` and Euler angles (`beta, gama, teta`) from `restpars(irest,4:6)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L122-L125).

**Coordinate Transformation**: Fixed molecules are rotated using `call eulerfixed(beta,gama,teta,v1,v2,v3)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L129) which generates the rotation matrix from Euler angles. The transformation applies the rotation matrix to each atom's coordinates and translates to the target center of mass [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L134-L143).

**Validation Checks**: The program enforces constraints that fixed molecules cannot have `nmols(itype) > 1` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L148-L152) and cannot use restart files [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L153-L158). The `fixed(itype)` logical array marks which molecule types are immobile [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L147).

**Array Reorganization**: To optimize subsequent operations, fixed molecules are moved to the end of the molecule type arrays. A bubble-sort-like operation swaps fixed molecule data with free molecule data, ensuring all free molecules occupy indices `1:ntype` while fixed molecules occupy `ntype+1:ntype_with_fixed` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L186-L247). This reorganization enables efficient subset operations during optimization.

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L114-L247)

## Phase 3: Parameter Setup

The parameter setup phase configures all optimization parameters, tolerances, and constraints based on input specifications and computed properties.

**Variable Count Calculation**: The total number of optimization variables `n = ntotmol * 6` accounts for 3 translational and 3 rotational degrees of freedom per free molecule [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L264). The program distinguishes between `ntmol` (total molecules), `ntotmol` (free molecules), and `nfixedat` (fixed atoms) [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L256-L278).

**Tolerance Configuration**: Default tolerances are initialized with `radius(i) = dism/2.d0` and `fscale(i) = 1.d0` for all atoms [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L283-L284). Short-distance tolerances can be enabled globally or per-atom for specialized handling of specific atom pairs [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L285-L292).

**Atom-Specific Parameters**: The program processes molecule-specific radius, fscale, and short_radius specifications, first applying to all atoms in a molecule [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L317-L388), then overwriting with atom-specific values defined within `atoms...end` blocks [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L409-L515). This hierarchical approach enables both efficient default assignment and precise per-atom control.

**Validation**: Short radius specifications are validated to ensure `short_radius(i) < radius(i)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L519-L528), maintaining the hierarchical relationship between primary and secondary distance tolerances.

**Periodic Boundary Conditions**: When PBC is enabled, an additional box constraint is automatically added to keep non-fixed molecules within the simulation cell [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L537-L546). This constraint uses `pbc_min` and `pbc_max` to define the bounding region.

**Constraint Array Construction**: The `nratom(icart)` array tracks the number of geometric constraints applying to each atom, while `iratom(icart,i)` stores the indices of these constraints [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L548-L632). This enables efficient constraint evaluation during objective function computation.

**Rotation Constraints**: Rotational degrees of freedom can be constrained along specific axes using `constrain_rotation` keywords [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L634-L691). These bounds are converted from degrees to radians for internal calculations.

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L249-L691)

## Phase 4: Initial Configuration

The initial configuration phase creates the starting point for optimization and validates that a meaningful problem exists.

**All-Fixed Check**: If no free molecules exist (`n.eq.0`), the program directly outputs the fixed molecule configuration without optimization [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L695-L705). This handles the edge case of purely static arrangements.

**Initial Point Generation**: The `call initial(n,x)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L711) subroutine creates the initial optimization variable vector. This involves computing maximum internal distances for each molecule type, defining system boundaries based on spatial constraints, and generating random positions and orientations for free molecules [initial.f90](src/initial.f90#L10-L100).

**Initial Function Evaluation**: The program evaluates the objective function at the initial point using `call computef(n,x,all_type_fx)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L719). This provides a baseline for measuring optimization progress and validates that the initial configuration is physically reasonable.

**Check Mode**: When `check` mode is enabled, the program outputs the initial configuration and terminates without optimization, useful for debugging input files and verifying constraint definitions [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L728-L733).

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L694-L733), [initial.f90](src/initial.f90#L9-L559), [computef.f90](src/computef.f90#L9-L100)

## Phase 5: Main Packing Loop

The main packing loop implements Packmol's sophisticated two-phase optimization strategy that balances efficiency with convergence quality.

**Loop Architecture**: The outer `main` loop iterates through molecule types from `itype = 1` to `ntype + 1` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L742-L765). When `packall` is enabled, the loop jumps directly to `itype = ntype + 1`, packing all molecules together. The inner `gencanloop` performs repeated GENCAN optimization iterations for each phase [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L811-L961).

**Phase 1: Type-Specific Packing** (`itype ≤ ntype`): Each molecule type is optimized independently using `call swaptype(n,x,itype,1)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L756), which configures the optimization variables to include only molecules of the current type. This decoupling reduces problem complexity and accelerates convergence. After each optimization, the all-type function value is computed using `call swaptype(n,x,itype,3)` to restore all molecules [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L886-L888).

**Phase 2: Joint Packing** (`itype = ntype + 1`): All free molecules are optimized together using `call swaptype(n,x,itype,3)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L758). This final phase resolves any residual overlaps between different molecule types and fine-tunes the configuration for overall optimality.

**Radius Scaling Strategy**: An adaptive tolerance strategy improves convergence by initially using larger effective radii (`radscale = discale`) to achieve coarse separation, then gradually reducing to user-specified tolerances [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L748-L751). The scaling factor decreases when `fdist < precision` and improvement falls below thresholds [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L940-L948).

> [!TIP]
> The radius scaling mechanism is crucial for efficiency. By starting with inflated molecular radii (typically 10-20% larger than specified), the optimization quickly achieves a good packing layout, then progressively tightens tolerances to achieve the precise user-specified distances. This staged approach significantly reduces overall computation time for large systems.

**GENCAN Optimization**: Each iteration calls `call pgencan(n,x,fx)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L830), which invokes the GENCAN conjugate gradient method to minimize the objective function. The optimization operates on the active variable set defined by the current `swaptype` configuration.

**Bad Molecule Movement**: When enabled and convergence stalls, `call movebad(n,x,fx,movebadprint)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L817) displaces molecules with severe constraint violations, helping escape local minima. This heuristic operates only when `radscale == 1.d0` (final tolerance phase) and `fimp ≤ 10.d0` (low improvement).

**Convergence Testing**: After each GENCAN iteration, the program checks `fdist < precision` and `frest < precision` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L875) to determine if convergence criteria are met. When satisfied during type-specific packing, the program advances to the next type. When satisfied during joint packing, the optimization terminates successfully [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L896-L903).

**Progressive Output**: The program periodically writes the best configuration to the output file based on the `writeout` interval [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L909-L925). The `writebad` option forces output even of non-converged configurations, enabling progress inspection for difficult problems.

**Maximum Iteration Handling**: When `loop.eq.nloop` is reached, the program either advances to the next packing phase or terminates with a convergence error if this is the final phase [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L950-L959). A checkpoint file is written to enable resumption of long-running optimizations.

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L735-L965), [swaptypemod.f90](src/swaptypemod.f90#L10-L15)

## Phase 6: Termination and Output

The termination phase handles final output generation, cleanup, and program exit with appropriate status codes.

**Final Output**: Upon successful convergence, the program calls `call output(n,x,xyzout)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L877) to write the final molecular configuration. Success messages are generated via `call writesuccess(itype,fdist,frest,fx)` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L880), which logs final constraint violations and objective function values.

**Timing and Statistics**: The total execution time is reported as `etime(tarray) - time0` [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L967), providing users with performance metrics for their specific system configurations.

**Exit Code Handling**: The program terminates with status codes defined in the `exit_codes` module [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L972-L978). A normal exit returns code 0, while convergence failures return `exit_code_failed_to_converge`. Other error conditions return `exit_code_general_error` for proper integration with shell scripting and workflow pipelines.

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L967-L980), [exit_codes.f90](src/exit_codes.f90)

## Key Data Structures and Interfaces

The main program interfaces with several critical data structures that maintain the simulation state throughout execution.

**Optimization Vector `x(nn)`**: The primary optimization variable array stores 6 values per free molecule: `x(1:3)` for the center-of-mass position and `x(4:6)` for Euler angles (β, γ, θ). The variable ordering groups all translational parameters first, followed by all rotational parameters [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L256-L268).

**Coordinate Storage**: The `coor(ntotat,3)` array stores atomic coordinates in molecule-local reference frames, while `xcart(ntotat,3)` stores world-space coordinates computed during objective function evaluation [computef.f90](src/computef.f90#L72). This separation enables efficient coordinate transformations during optimization.

**Cell Indexing**: Spatial hashing via cell indexing enables efficient neighbor searching during overlap detection. The `latomfirst` and `latomnext` arrays implement linked lists of atoms within each spatial cell, reducing the computational complexity of distance calculations from O(N²) to approximately O(N) [computef.f90](src/computef.f90#L84-L96).

**Type Management**: The `swaptype` routine [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L740) manipulates variable and atom indices to enable optimization of molecule subsets. By temporarily reassigning `ntype`, `nmols`, and related arrays, the program can optimize specific molecule types independently while preserving the global coordinate system.

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L59-L77), [computef.f90](src/computef.f90#L17-L100)

## Phase Comparison Summary

| Phase | Purpose | Key Operations | Variables Active | Convergence Target |
|-------|---------|----------------|------------------|-------------------|
| Initialization | Setup and validation | Memory allocation, input parsing, coordinate centering | All types | N/A |
| Fixed Processing | Position reference structures | Rotation and translation of fixed molecules | All types | N/A |
| Parameter Setup | Configure optimization tolerances | Radius assignment, constraint array construction | All types | N/A |
| Initial Config | Generate starting point | Random positions and orientations | Free types only | N/A |
| Type-Specific Packing | Separate each molecule type | GENCAN optimization per type | Single type | `fdist < precision`, `frest < precision` |
| Joint Packing | Final refinement | GENCAN optimization with all types | All free types | `fdist < precision`, `frest < precision` |
| Termination | Output and cleanup | File writing, statistics reporting | N/A | N/A |

## Performance Considerations

The execution flow design addresses several computational challenges inherent to molecular packing:

**Scalability**: The cell indexing system enables near-linear scaling with system size by limiting pairwise distance checks to spatially proximate atoms. The `radmax` parameter [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L532-L535) determines cell dimensions based on the largest molecular radius.

**Memory Efficiency**: The program uses precise dimensioning based on input specifications rather than fixed maximum sizes. The `setsizes()` routine calculates optimal array dimensions, minimizing memory footprint while maintaining safety margins.

**Adaptive Complexity**: The two-phase packing strategy reduces problem complexity by isolating type-specific overlaps before addressing inter-type overlaps. This decomposition reduces the search space dimensionality and accelerates convergence for heterogeneous systems.

> [!TIP]
> For very large systems (>10,000 molecules), consider using the `nloop_type` parameter to increase iterations during type-specific packing. This allows each type to achieve better convergence before the more expensive joint packing phase begins. The `packall` option can be used to skip type-specific packing for simpler homogeneous systems.

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L746-L759), [cell_indexing.f90](src/cell_indexing.f90)

## Error Handling and Validation

The program implements comprehensive validation at each execution phase:

**Input Validation**: Fixed molecule constraints are checked for consistency with molecule count and restart file usage [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L148-L158). Atom selections in parameter specifications are validated against molecule sizes [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L423-L426).

**Constraint Verification**: The program ensures each movable molecule has at least one geometric constraint defined [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L626-L630), preventing unconstrained degrees of freedom that would lead to divergence.

**Radius Validation**: Short radius specifications are validated to maintain the hierarchical relationship with primary radii [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L519-L528), ensuring consistent constraint application.

**Convergence Validation**: The program explicitly checks that initial approximations are valid solutions when appropriate [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L775-L780), preventing unnecessary optimization when constraints are already satisfied.

Sources: [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L148-L158), [packmol.f90](app/packmol.f90#L626-L630)

- **Optimization Algorithm**: Refer to [GENCAN Optimization Method Overview](9-gencan-optimization-method-overview) for understanding the mathematical foundations of the optimization method
- **Objective Function**: Study [Objective Function Design in computef.f90](10-objective-function-design-in-computef-f90) to understand how constraints are evaluated and penalized
- **Coordinate Systems**: Review [Molecular Coordinate Systems: Baricenter and Euler Angles](13-molecular-coordinate-systems-baricenter-and-euler-angles) for details on coordinate transformations
- **Restart Mechanism**: See [Checkpoint and Restart Mechanism](23-checkpoint-and-restart-mechanism) for understanding how long-running optimizations can be resumed


# Input Parsing and Parameter Validation



Packmol's input parsing and parameter validation system forms the critical first line of defense against configuration errors, implementing a multi-layered validation approach that spans command-line processing, file I/O, keyword recognition, and constraint verification. This system processes user input through three distinct stages—command-line parsing, file reading and tokenization, and semantic validation—before any molecular packing calculations commence.

## Command-Line Argument Processing

The parsing architecture supports three execution modes for flexible integration with different workflow paradigms. The `cli_parser` module implements a strict validation scheme that accepts only specific argument patterns, rejecting ambiguous or malformed invocations immediately with detailed error messages [Sources: src/cli_parser.f90#L1-L100].

**Supported Execution Modes:**

| Mode | Arguments | Input Source | Output Source |
|------|-----------|--------------|---------------|
| Standard Input | `packmol` | stdin | specified in input file |
| Single File | `packmol -i input.inp` | input.inp | specified in input file |
| Both Files | `packmol -i input.inp -o output.pdb` | input.inp | output.pdb |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[packmol execution] --> B{Argument count?}
    B -->|0| C[stdin redirection mode]
    B -->|2| D[Input file mode]
    B -->|4| E[Both files mode]
    B -->|Other| F[Error: Invalid arguments]
    D --> G{First argument?}
    G -->|-i| H[Parse input filename]
    G -->|Other| F
    E --> I[Parse -i input.inp]
    E --> J[Parse -o output.pdb]
    H --> K[Validate filename not empty]
    I --> K
    J --> L[Validate filenames differ]
    K --> M[Proceed to file parsing]
    L --> M
    C --> M
```

The parser enforces strict separation of concerns: input and output filenames must be distinct paths, and only recognized flags (`-i`, `-o`) are permitted. Any deviation triggers an immediate termination with exit code `exit_code_command_line_error` (174) and displays usage examples to guide users toward correct invocation [Sources: src/cli_parser.f90#L100-L242].

## Input File Reading and Tokenization

The `setsizes` subroutine initiates the file parsing process by determining array dimensions and establishing the input file structure. This two-phase approach—first counting, then allocating—ensures memory efficiency by allocating precisely sized arrays rather than overestimating requirements [Sources: src/setsizes.f90#L1-L200].

The parsing pipeline handles several preprocessing tasks:

1. **Comment Stripping**: Lines beginning with `#` or containing `#` have comments removed, with trailing blank characters preserved to maintain line structure
2. **Whitespace Normalization**: All non-standard blank characters convert to standard spaces, ensuring consistent tokenization across different text editors and operating systems
3. **Quote-Aware Path Handling**: Filenames with spaces are wrapped in quotes and temporarily marked with `@` delimiters during tokenization, then reconstructed during keyword extraction [Sources: src/setsizes.f90#L50-L120]

The `keyword(nlines, maxkeywords)` array stores all parsed tokens, with `maxkeywords` dynamically determined during the initial counting pass. This 2D array enables efficient keyword access by line number during subsequent validation phases [Sources: src/setsizes.f90#L120-L160].

## Global Parameter Validation

The `getinp` subroutine performs comprehensive validation of all global parameters before structure-specific processing begins. This establishes baseline system configuration and validates file access patterns [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L1-L100].

**Primary Global Parameters:**

| Parameter | Default | Validation | Usage |
|-----------|---------|------------|-------|
| `tolerance` | Required | Must be positive | Minimum intermolecular distance |
| `filetype` | pdb | pdb, xyz, or tinker | Structure file format |
| `output` | Required | Valid filename path | Output coordinate file |
| `seed` | 1234567 | Integer, -1 triggers time-based | Random number generator seed |
| `precision` | 1.d-2 | Positive real number | Convergence tolerance |
| `discale` | 1.1d0 | Positive real number | Initial tolerance scaling factor |
| `maxit` | 20 | Positive integer | Maximum optimization iterations |
| `nloop` | 0 | Non-negative integer | Constraint enforcement loops |
| `writeout` | 10 | Positive integer | Output frequency (iterations) |

> [!TIP]
> The seed parameter accepts special value `-1` to trigger automatic seeding from system time via `seed_from_time` subroutine, ensuring different random configurations across runs without manual intervention.

Keyword validation employs an exhaustive whitelist approach: any unrecognized keyword triggers immediate termination with `exit_code_input_error` (171). The whitelist contains approximately 40 valid keywords, including both global parameters and structure-specific directives [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L100-L200].

## Structure Block Parsing

Each molecular type definition resides within a `structure`...`end structure` block, which the parser identifies and processes sequentially. The parsing maintains a `inside_structure` logical flag to track context, enabling proper scoping of keywords that are valid only within structure definitions [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L1-L100].

**Structure Block Keywords:**

| Category | Keywords | Validation Rules |
|----------|----------|------------------|
| Definition | `structure filename` | File must exist and match declared filetype |
| Quantity | `number N` | N must be positive integer |
| Spatial | `inside box/outside box` | Six coordinates: x1 y1 z1 x2 y2 z2 |
| Spatial | `inside sphere/outside sphere` | Four coordinates: x y z radius |
| Fixed | `fixed x y z α β γ` | Three coordinates, three Euler angles |
| Centering | `center`, `centerofmass` | Mutually exclusive options |
| Rotational | `constrain_rotation axis min max` | Axis: x/y/z, bounds: 0-360 degrees |
| Output | `resnumbers N`, `chain C`, `segid S` | N: integer, C: single char, S: 4-char string |

Fixed molecule validation includes critical constraints: fixed molecules must have `number 1`, and restart files cannot be combined with fixed positioning. These restrictions prevent logical inconsistencies in the optimization problem formulation [Sources: app/packmol.f90#L100-L200].

## Coordinate File Format Reading

Packmol supports three coordinate file formats, each with specific parsing routines and validation checks. The file format determination occurs through the global `filetype` keyword, defaulting to PDB format if unspecified [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L200-L400].

### PDB Format

PDB parsing validates strict column-based formatting according to PDB specification standards. Key validation checks include:

- **Coordinate columns**: Positions must be in columns 31-38, 39-46, 47-54 for x, y, z respectively
- **Residue numbers**: Must be parseable integers in columns 23-26, used for output formatting only
- **Atom records**: Only `ATOM` and `HETATM` records are processed; all others skipped
- **Connectivity**: Optional `CONECT` records read with index adjustment based on first atom number [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L300-L400]

> [!TIP]
> PDB connectivity information is optional and only preserved if present in input files. When `connect` parameter is set to `no` within structure blocks, all CONECT records are ignored regardless of input file contents.

### XYZ Format

XYZ format parsing follows the simpler three-line-per-atom structure: first line contains atom count, second line contains molecule title, subsequent lines contain element symbol and coordinates. This format lacks connectivity information and chain/residue metadata [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L450-L500].

### TINKER Format

TINKER format parsing includes an initial line with atom count and molecule title, followed by one line per atom containing atomic number, element symbol, x/y/z coordinates, and connectivity list. The `setcon` subroutine pre-processes files to determine connection counts before full coordinate reading [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L500-L600, src/getinp.f90#L1000-L1100].

## Constraint Syntax Validation

Spatial constraints undergo coordinate range and geometric validation during parsing. The parser converts constraint definitions into standardized parameter arrays used during optimization [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L700-L800].

**Constraint Parameter Storage:**

The `restpars(irest, 1:6)` array stores constraint parameters with the following indexing:
- Index 1-3: Primary spatial coordinates (origin for box/sphere, plane equation coefficients)
- Index 4-6: Secondary coordinates (opposite box corner for box constraints, rotation angles for fixed molecules)

Specialized constraints (gaussian distributions, cylindrical constraints) extend this storage to include width parameters in indices 5-6 [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L700-L800].

## Error Handling Architecture

Packmol employs a structured error code system that distinguishes between different failure modes, enabling precise error reporting and automated error handling in batch workflows [Sources: src/exit_codes.f90#L1-L20].

**Error Code Classification:**

| Code | Constant | Typical Trigger |
|------|----------|-----------------|
| 0 | exit_code_success | Successful completion |
| 171 | exit_code_input_error | Invalid keywords, malformed constraints |
| 172 | exit_code_open_file | Missing structure files, invalid paths |
| 173 | exit_code_failed_to_converge | Optimization exceeded maxit iterations |
| 174 | exit_code_command_line_error | Invalid CLI argument combinations |

File opening failures invoke the `failopen` subroutine, which provides context-aware error messages including the specific filename and suggestions for troubleshooting path issues [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L900-L1000].

## Validation Flow Integration

The complete parsing sequence integrates with the main program flow through well-defined entry points. The `packmol.f90` main program orchestrates the parsing pipeline: command-line parsing precedes file reading, which precedes structure validation, enabling early detection of configuration errors before memory-intensive operations [Sources: app/packmol.f90#L1-L100].

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CLI as cli_parser
    participant SS as setsizes
    participant GI as getinp
    participant FS as failopen
    participant Main as packmol

    Main->>CLI: parse_command_line_args()
    CLI-->>Main: input_file_name, output_file_name

    Main->>SS: setsizes()
    SS->>SS: Read & tokenize input file
    SS->>SS: Count lines & allocate arrays
    SS->>SS: Extract keywords
    SS-->>Main: Allocated data structures

    Main->>GI: getinp()
    GI->>GI: Validate global parameters
    GI->>GI: Parse structure blocks
    loop Each structure file
        GI->>FS: Open structure file
        alt File exists
            FS-->>GI: File handle
            GI->>GI: Read coordinates
        else File missing
            FS-->>Main: exit_code_open_file
        end
    end
    GI->>GI: Validate constraints
    GI-->>Main: Validated configuration

    Main->>Main: Proceed to optimization
```

## Practical Validation Patterns

The test suite provides validated input file examples demonstrating correct parameter usage across various scenarios [Sources: testing/input_files/].

**Simple Box Packing:**

```fortran
tolerance 2.0
filetype pdb
output output.pdb

structure ./structure_files/water.pdb
  number 1000
  inside box -20. -20. -20. 20. 20. 20.
end structure
```

**Fixed Molecules with Explicit Positioning:**

```fortran
tolerance 2.0

structure ./structure_files/SOD.pdb
  number 1 
  fixed 0. 0. -1. 0. 0. 0.
  centerofmass
end structure

structure ./structure_files/SOD.pdb
  number 1 
  fixed 0. 0. 1. 0. 0. 0.
  centerofmass
end structure
```

Note the validation rule that `number` must be 1 for fixed molecules, enforced by the parser to prevent logical contradictions in constraint specification [Sources: testing/input_files/toy_with_fixed.inp].

**Complex Multi-Component System:**

```fortran
tolerance 2.0

structure ./structure_files/protein.pdb
  resnumbers 0
  number 1 
  fixed 0. 0. 0. 0. 0. 0.
  centerofmass
end structure

structure ./structure_files/water.pdb
  resnumbers 2
  number 1000 
  inside sphere 0. 0. 0. 50.
end structure
```

This example demonstrates mixing fixed molecules (number=1, explicit coordinates) with mobile molecules (number>1, spatial constraints), all within a single input file [Sources: testing/input_files/solvprotein.inp].

## Advanced Validation Features

**Restart File Validation:**

Restart file specifications can occur at global scope (affecting all structures) or within individual structure blocks (affecting only that molecule type). The parser validates that restart_from and restart_to specifications don't conflict with fixed molecule declarations, as fixed molecules cannot have restart configurations [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L900-L1000].

**PBC Parameter Validation:**

Periodic boundary condition validation ensures positive box dimensions and properly defined coordinate ranges. The parser checks that `pbc_length = pbc_max - pbc_min` is positive in all directions, rejecting degenerate or inverted boxes immediately [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L150-L200].

**Short Tolerance Validation:**

The `short_tol_dist` parameter (used for specialized close-contact penalties) must satisfy `short_tol_dist < tolerance`. This constraint ensures mathematical consistency in the multi-scale penalty function implementation [Sources: src/getinp.f90#L800-L900].

## Summary

Packmol's input parsing and parameter validation system implements a defense-in-depth approach, catching configuration errors at multiple stages from command-line invocation through constraint validation. The architecture prioritizes fail-fast behavior with detailed error messages, enabling users to rapidly identify and correct configuration issues before resource-intensive optimization calculations begin. For deeper understanding of how validated parameters are used in optimization algorithms, refer to [GENCAN Optimization Method Overview](9-gencan-optimization-method-overview). For practical examples of input file construction across different scenarios, explore [Building Simple Water Boxes](25-building-simple-water-boxes) and [Solvating Proteins with Ions](27-solvating-proteins-with-ions).

# Checkpoint and Restart Mechanism



The checkpoint mechanism in Packmol represents a **failure recovery strategy** rather than traditional checkpoint-restart functionality. When the optimizer exhausts its iteration budget without achieving convergence, Packmol invokes checkpoint procedures to preserve the best partial solution and provide actionable diagnostic information. This mechanism ensures users receive useful output even when ideal packing cannot be achieved within computational constraints.

## Checkpoint Invocation Conditions

The checkpoint subroutine is triggered when the GENCAN optimization loop reaches the maximum number of iterations (`nloop`) without satisfying convergence criteria. This occurs specifically at the final stage of packing when processing all molecules together, as evidenced in the main program flow [packmol.f90](/app/packmol.f90#L950-L959). The system tracks iteration progress through a loop counter (`loop`) that increments with each GENCAN optimization cycle, comparing against the configured `nloop` threshold.

When this condition is met during the final packing phase (when `itype == ntype+1`), the program invokes the checkpoint mechanism with the best-known solution vector stored in `xprint`, then exits with a failure convergence status code. This design ensures that users receive meaningful output rather than encountering a complete failure state without diagnostic information.

## Checkpoint Subroutine Architecture
